title: Explain the class-loader delegation (parent delegation) model, and give a scenario where it causes issues (same class, two loaders → ClassCastException).
shortTitle: What is the class-loader delegation model?

s1_definition.profdef: The parent delegation model is the rule that, before a class loader tries to load a class itself, it first asks its parent loader to load it, and the parent asks its own parent, all the way up to the Bootstrap loader. Only if every ancestor fails to find the class does the original loader attempt to load it. This guarantees that core classes are always loaded by the most trusted loader and that a given class is loaded once per loader, preventing accidental duplication or malicious replacement of core types. It can still cause problems when the same class is loaded by two independent loaders, producing two distinct runtime types that are incompatible.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a new junior librarian at National Bank of India is asked for the Account blueprint. Before touching their own shelf, they are required to ask their senior, who asks the chief librarian, who checks the most trusted vault first. Only if nobody above has it does the junior finally look on their own shelf. This protects the bank, because nobody can sneak a fake "Account" blueprint onto a lower shelf and have it override the real one from the trusted vault. The trouble starts if two separate branches of the bank each independently print their own Account blueprint; a form filled using one branch's blueprint will be rejected by the other branch even though both are called Account.
s1_definition.oneliner: Delegation means a loader asks its parent first and only loads a class itself as a last resort, which protects core classes but means the same class from two loaders becomes two incompatible types.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The parent delegation model is the rule that, before a class loader tries to load a class itself, it first asks its parent loader to load it, and the parent asks its own parent, all the way up to the Bootstrap loader. Only if every ancestor fails to find the class does the original loader attempt to load it. This guarantees that core classes are always loaded by the most trusted loader and that a given class is loaded once per loader, preventing accidental duplication or malicious replacement of core types. It can still cause problems when the same class is loaded by two independent loaders, producing two distinct runtime types that are incompatible.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a new junior librarian at National Bank of India is asked for the Account blueprint. Before touching their own shelf, they are required to ask their senior, who asks the chief librarian, who checks the most trusted vault first. Only if nobody above has it does the junior finally look on their own shelf. This protects the bank, because nobody can sneak a fake "Account" blueprint onto a lower shelf and have it override the real one from the trusted vault. The trouble starts if two separate branches of the bank each independently print their own Account blueprint; a form filled using one branch's blueprint will be rejected by the other branch even though both are called Account.

**One line to remember:** Delegation means a loader asks its parent first and only loads a class itself as a last resort, which protects core classes but means the same class from two loaders becomes two incompatible types.

sections.s2_technical:
When you call `loadClass`, the default implementation in `ClassLoader` follows a fixed sequence. First it checks whether it has already loaded the class, using `findLoadedClass`. If not, it delegates to its parent by calling the parent's `loadClass`. The parent repeats the same logic, so the request bubbles all the way up to Bootstrap. Only when every ancestor reports that it cannot find the class does the current loader call its own `findClass` to actually load it. This upward-first order is why it is called parent delegation.

The first benefit is safety. Because core classes are always found by the Bootstrap loader at the top, no lower loader can substitute its own version of, say, java.lang.String. If delegation did not exist, a malicious or buggy jar could ship a fake String class and the JVM might load it, which would be a serious security hole. Delegation makes the core classes unforgeable.

The second benefit is uniqueness per loader. A class is identified in the JVM not just by its fully qualified name but by the combination of its name and the loader that defined it. Delegation ensures that within one loader chain, a class like Account is defined exactly once, so everyone shares the same Class object and instances are mutually assignable.

The problem scenario is two independent loaders that both define the same class. Suppose an application server loads a shared Account class in a common loader, but a web application also bundles its own copy of Account and a child loader defines it again instead of delegating. Now there are two Account types: Account defined by loader A and Account defined by loader B. An object created by one cannot be cast to the other, and you get a confusing `ClassCastException` whose message looks like Account cannot be cast to Account, which baffles developers because the names are identical. The fix is to make the class available only in the shared parent loader so both sides delegate to it, or to deliberately break delegation only where you truly intend isolation. A senior nuance is that some frameworks intentionally invert delegation, such as web containers loading web-app classes before parent classes to support independent versions, and the thread context class loader exists precisely to bridge the gaps this creates for service loading.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India deployed a plugin that accidentally bundled its own copy of the shared Account class. At runtime, the core TransferService expected the shared Account, but the plugin handed it an Account created by the plugin's own loader. The cast failed with a ClassCastException that said Account cannot be cast to Account, and the on-call engineer lost hours because the names looked identical. This is exactly the two-loaders problem, because the same class name defined by two different loaders is two different types.

Problem 2 — The team wanted to prove that normal delegation keeps a class unique. When both the core and a well-behaved plugin delegate loading of Account up to the shared parent, they end up using the same Class object, and casting works fine. This is exactly the benefit of parent delegation, and demonstrating both the broken and the correct path makes the rule memorable.

In the mini-project we simulate the problem with two custom loaders that each define their own copy of a small `Ledger` class, and show that an instance from one cannot be cast or assigned to the type seen by the other, reproducing the confusing ClassCastException. We then show the correct path where both delegate to the shared application loader and the cast succeeds. The demo uses Rajesh and Priya conceptually as the data the Ledger holds and logs each loader and the outcome.


sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a request to load the class com.bank.deleg.Ledger through two separate isolating loaders, loaderA and loaderB, and then through the shared application loader twice.

Step 1: loaderA.loadClass is called for Ledger. Because Ledger is its target, loaderA skips delegation, reads the Ledger bytecode itself, and calls defineClass, producing a Class object we call ledgerA owned by loaderA.

Step 2: loaderB.loadClass is called for the same name. loaderB also skips delegation for its target, reads the same bytecode, and defines its own Class object, ledgerB, owned by loaderB. Now there are two Ledger types in the JVM, identical in name and bytes but different in identity.

Step 3: LoaderReport.compare logs the loader of each and the result of ledgerA equals ledgerB by reference, which is false. This proves identity in the JVM is name plus loader, not name alone.

Step 4: The demo creates an instance from ledgerA and tries to cast it to ledgerB. The JVM checks types by identity, sees they are different types, and throws a ClassCastException whose message confusingly reports Ledger cannot be cast to Ledger. This reproduces the exact production puzzle.

Step 5: The demo then loads Ledger twice through the shared application loader using Class.forName. Because both calls delegate normally and the application loader defines Ledger only once, both calls return the very same Class object, so the reference comparison is true and casting would succeed. This shows the correct, delegation-respecting path.

```text
[INFO] A loaded by: com.bank.deleg.IsolatingLoader@...
[INFO] B loaded by: com.bank.deleg.IsolatingLoader@...
[INFO] Same Class object? false
[SEVERE] ClassCastException reproduced: class com.bank.deleg.Ledger cannot be cast to class com.bank.deleg.Ledger  (same name, two loaders = two types)
[INFO] Shared loader gives one type? true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Request: load com.bank.deleg.Ledger
    │
    ├─ BROKEN PATH (two isolating loaders)        ├─ CORRECT PATH (delegation)
    │  loaderA.defineClass → LedgerA               │  AppLoader asked first
    │  loaderB.defineClass → LedgerB               │  (delegates up, defines once)
    │  LedgerA != LedgerB  (two types)             │  Class.forName twice → SAME type
    │  cast A→B  → ClassCastException              │  cast succeeds
    ▼                                              ▼
  "Ledger cannot be cast to Ledger"              one shared Class object

  Delegation order (default loadClass):
    findLoadedClass → parent.loadClass → ... → Bootstrap → then findClass (self)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Plugin Isolation vs Shared Types ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Banking App Server (JVM)                     │
  │  AppClassLoader (shared)                       │
  │    └─ Account, Ledger, TransferService (ONE)   │
  │         ▲                      ▲                │
  │   delegates up           delegates up          │
  │         │                      │                │

  BUG: if a plugin bundles its own Ledger and defines it locally →

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Parent Delegation ═══

  ── Sequence: default loadClass(name) ──
  1. findLoadedClass(name)        already loaded? return it
  2. parent.loadClass(name)       ASK PARENT FIRST (recursive to Bootstrap)
  3. if parent failed:
  4.    findClass(name)           load it MYSELF (last resort)
  5.    defineClass(bytes)        name + THIS loader = unique type

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<abstract>> ClassLoader   │
  │  + loadClass(name): Class    │  template: delegate then findClass
  │  # findClass(name): Class    │  override to customize
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
      extends      │
                   ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │        IsolatingLoader        │
  │  - target: String             │
  │  + loadClass(name): Class     │  breaks delegation ONLY for target
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Identity rule: a Class is (fully-qualified name, defining loader).
  Two loaders → two identities → cast between them fails.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The parent delegation model is the rule that, before a class loader tries to load a class on its own, it first delegates the request to its parent loader, and that parent delegates to its parent, all the way up to the Bootstrap loader. Only if every ancestor reports that it cannot find the class does the original loader finally load it itself with findClass. That is why it is called parent delegation: the request always travels upward first and loading happens as a last resort at the lowest level.

This design gives two important guarantees. The first is security, because core classes like java.lang.String are always found by the trusted Bootstrap loader at the top, so no lower loader or malicious jar can substitute a fake version of a core type. The second is uniqueness, because within one loader chain a class is defined exactly once, so everyone shares the same Class object and instances are mutually assignable. The key fact underneath all of this is that the JVM identifies a class by the combination of its fully qualified name and the loader that defined it, not by the name alone.

That identity rule is exactly where the classic problem appears. If the same class name is defined by two independent loaders, the JVM treats them as two completely different types. An object created under one loader's version cannot be cast or assigned to the other loader's version, and you get a ClassCastException whose message bizarrely says something like Account cannot be cast to Account, which confuses everyone because the names are identical. In my banking work this happened when a plugin accidentally bundled its own copy of the shared Account class and defined it in its own loader instead of delegating, so when it handed an object back to the core TransferService the cast blew up.

The fix is to keep shared classes available only in the common parent loader so every child delegates to the single definition, and to break delegation only where genuine isolation is intended. One senior nuance I always add is that some frameworks deliberately invert delegation, like web containers that load web-application classes before parent classes so each app can carry its own library versions, and that the thread context class loader exists precisely to bridge the gaps this inversion creates for service loading. So my complete answer is that parent delegation asks the parent first and loads locally only as a last resort, which keeps core classes safe and unique, but because class identity is name plus loader, defining the same class in two loaders creates two incompatible types and the confusing same-name ClassCastException.

---

keyPoints: Child delegates to parent FIRST — parent tries to load before child
Prevents duplicate class loading — same class loaded once
If parent cannot find it, child attempts to load
Violation: if two loaders load the same class, they are different types — ClassCastException
Tomcat breaks delegation intentionally — loads webapp classes before parent
